full_judgment:
2. In this case, the petitioner is the father of the victim of Kaligonj PS Case No.11 dated 14-8-2000. The petitioner prayed for giving custody of the victim girl to him and his prayer was not considered by the learned Sessions Judge, Satkhira in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 577 of 2000 and by his order dated 1-11-2000 the learned Sessions Judge rejected the prayer and passed an order for keeping her in safe custody. The victim girl also made a prayer for allowing her to go with her husband, the accused of the above case. The learned Sessions Judge also rejected that prayer. The petitioner then moved this court by filing the present application under section 491 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. 

 3. The learned Advocate, Mr Probir Halder who appeared on behalf of the petitioner, has submitted that the victim is a minor girl and, as such, the petitioner, father of the victim is entitled to get custody of the victim. He was asked to enlighten us on the question whether a person put into judicial custody by a competent court can be set at liberty under the provisions of section 491 of the Code and also on the question whether custody of a minor can be determined in an application under section 491 of the Code. Mr Halder has submitted that such applications are being entertained by this court and, as such, though there is no decision on the above question, the questions may be determined in this application under section 491 of the Code. In this connection, he has referred to the case of BADC vs Kibria and Associates Ltd reported in 46 DLR (AD) 97 and has invited our attention to the observations of the court made at paragraph 18 of that reported case. He has argued that there is uniform decision in this Court on the above questions and, as such, though there is no legislative backing, the decisions of the Superior Courts ripen into law. He has further argued that though the questions were not actually agitated in any case, from the decisions given by this court in cases under section 491 of the Code, the questions raised can be decided in a case under section 491. He has also referred to Article 111 of the Constitution of Bangladesh to impress upon us that the law declared by the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court is binding on all other courts. 

 4. We have perused the application under section 491. The petitioner claimed that the detenu is his minor daughter and, as such, the learned Sessions Judge acted illegally in refusing his prayer for giving her custody to him and in passing an order for judicial custody to the girl. In the cause title of the present application, it has been clearly mentioned that the detenu is detained in safe custody pursuant to an order dated 1-11-2000 passed by the learned Sessions Judge, Satkhira in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 577 of 2000. So, it is obvious that the detenu was put into judicial custody in view of the order passed by the learned Sessions Judge, Satkhira. We are of the view that so long this order of the learned Sessions Judge, Satkhira stands and is not set aside by any Superior Court, it cannot be said that the victim was put into judicial custody illegally or improperly. The validity of the order passed by the learned Sessions Judge can be set aside only by a superior Court in appeal or revision, as the case may be, but this court while exercising its jurisdiction of Habeas Corpus under section 491 cannot act either as appellate Court or cannot exercise revisional jurisdiction. In exercising the power of Habeas Corpus, the court can only determine whether detention of a person is illegal or improper, not beyond that. So, we are of the view that unless and until the order passed by the learned Sessions Judge is set aside by a competent Superior Court, the legality or propriety of the order cannot be decided in this proceeding under section 491. 

 5. We have noticed that while expounding the principle of "implied power" submissions were made in the reported case regarding the uniform decisions followed by the court on a particular point and it was held that if uniformly followed, the decisions shall ripen into law. In the same paragraph 18, the court also observed that on an important matter, legislation is necessary, Moreover, we are of the view that the principle laid down and the observations made in that case have no manner of application in the present case before us because here the question of 'implied power' of the court has not been raised. 

 6. Mr Probir Halder has frankly admitted that there is no decisions of the Appellate Division exactly on the questions raised but he has argued that it is implied in some decisions that the questions may be considered in a proceeding under section 491 of the Code. Under Article 111 of the Constitution, law declared by the Appellate Division is binding on all other courts. Regarding the above question we have found no decision of our Appellate Division and Mr Halder also could not show us any decision. However, similar question arose in some cases before the Indian and Pakistani High Courts where it was decided that when a person was put into judicial custody by an order of a competent court of law, unless and until that order is set aside, detention cannot be considered as illegal under section 491 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. In this connection, we may refer to a case of Madras High Court reported in 33 Criminal Law Journal, page 49. In this case custody of an illegitimate child of a mother was not given to the mother by the lower court and then the mother moved the High Court under section 491 of the Code. The High Court held that the order was passed by a competent court and so long the order stands, the mother cannot get remedy under section 491. In .another case reported in 1982 P Criminal Law Journal page 1029 (Karachi), the detenu was handed over to the custody of the respondent by an order passed by an Additional City Magistrate. The High Court held that as the detenu was handed over to respondent by a competent court, application under section 491 was not maintainable unless the order of the Additional City Magistrate was set aside by a competent Court. In view of the provisions of section 491(1)(b) we are of the view that the present application under section 491 is not maintainable as the detenu was put into custody by an order of the learned Sessions Judge, Satkhira and as the same order is still in force. 

 (2) The Supreme Court may, from time to time, frame rules to regulate the procedure in cases under this section.
